stories.headline: AgentRun Adds Durable Execution and Self-Improvement to Agent Harnesses
stories.summary: AgentRun is an open-source platform under the Apache-2.0 license designed to overlay durable execution and state retention onto harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and pi. At the end of a run, the agent proposes notes, skills, or learned workflows, which are validated by code checks and a grader before being committed to a git repository for subsequent runs. In real-world testing, custom reviewers built on the platform dropped code review costs from Greptile's $1.00 rate to $0.18 per review while catching 1.6x the real bugs on unseen PRs. The system also includes spend caps, human-in-the-loop approvals, and Docker sandboxes.
stories.why_it_matters: Combines state retention, learned tool caching, and crash recovery into a manageable harness wrapper to control token spend.
stories.reason: AgentRun is a new open-source managed agent platform designed to provide self-improving execution environments and harnesses for AI agents.

See how ↓ Quickstart · Case studies · Tour · Templates · Deploy · Docs AgentRun is an open-source platform that supercharges your agents. It adds self-improvement, durable execution and a control plane on top of your favorite agent harness. Your agents become smarter, more fault tolerant and use fewer tokens with every run. An agent's Learning tab: what it kept, and what changed since. Demo data from the console's recorded fixtures. Code review. Greptile started charging a dollar a review in March, then our agents took off, and our bill went from $180 a month to $6,451. Give an agent a job it has done a hundred times and it rediscovers the same API, rereads the same docs and rebuilds the same plan, and you pay for every token of it. Bring your agent on the harness it runs best on: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or pi. AgentRun does everything around it: - It learns the work. After each run, the agent keeps what will help next time: a note, a skill, or a workflow that does the job without the loop. The next run starts from there. - It never loses a run. Every run lives in one store. Kill the server mid-run, start it again, and the run carries on. Give each agent the computer the job needs: a sandbox, a Linux desktop, an Android phone or a browser. - You stay in control. Approvals, spend caps and one console for every agent: what needs you, what failed, what's running and what it cost. Apache-2.0. Rather have your coding agent do it? Tell it: Read agentrun.ai/SKILL.md and set up AgentRun for me. Mission Control opens first: what needs you, what failed, what's running and what it cost, by day, by harness and by tool. Every agent is an API. Start a run from the Playground, then copy the same request into your code. You stay in control. An agent can stop and ask you, and the run waits until you answer. Turn it on with "learning": true in an agent's definition. At the end of every run, the agent gets one more turn to say what it would keep. stories.headline: Agent 'Maya Discovery' Highlights Verification Failure Modes in Research
stories.summary: A Google researcher deployed 48 AI agents over NASA lidar data and announced the discovery of an unmapped Maya village in Mexico after official databases returned no record. The incident illustrates how domain-specific evaluation and verification protocols remain critical when deploying agents into scientific discovery.

item.content:
Armed with a team of AI agents, Google researcher Pietro Miotti claimed earlier this week to have discovered a potentially unmapped Maya site in Mexico. There was just one problem: The site had already been discovered and was published in an academic journal last year. The incident, which sparked criticism among archeologists online, underscores a growing tension in science as amateurs wielding increasingly powerful AI tools parachute into specialist fields, often without the expertise needed to understand what they are looking at.
No, AI agents did not discover a previously unknown Maya site
Scientists are getting tired of amateurs parachuting into their fields and making ‘discoveries’ with AI.
Local communities are often already well aware of sites in their area.
Miotti said the idea to use AI to search for archeological sites came to him while traveling in Peru, when he began wondering what historic explorers might do with access to modern technology. He settled on lidar, a laser-based mapping technology that can produce detailed three-dimensional images of the environment, and set a team of 48 AI agents to comb through NASA lidar data for signs of undocumented sites. As “Peru isn’t well covered” by public lidar data, Miotti wrote, he shifted his focus to the Maya region.
The agents flagged numerous promising locations, including “one major village [that] doesn’t seem to have been registered” in existing records. Miotti, who described the research to The Verge as a personal side project done without any Google compute or resources, said he then reached out to Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) to check whether the apparent discovery was already known, including through unpublished research. Using the agents to translate his correspondence into Spanish, Miotti said INAH told him it had no record of a registered site at that location.
“It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive,” Miotti wrote on his blog.
Miotti stressed that he is not an archeologist and emphasized that the finding would need to be verified with fieldwork. Nevertheless, he hailed it as proof that “we’re on the brink of a revolution across every science” and called for the “entire planet” to be mapped with lidar so AI agents could “help us find the rest.” Had he been an archaeologist familiar with the region, however, Miotti might have spotted a problem: The site was already known, and had been documented in an academic journal more than a year earlier.
“I didn’t expect it to get this much attention.”
Archeologists were quick to point out the oversight on social media. In a series of posts on Bluesky, Sarah Parcak, an archeology professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, stressed the importance of carefully checking findings against existing research. “This is why we have peer review,” Parcak wrote, adding that just because the Mexican government doesn’t have something in its database doesn’t mean it is unknown or unmapped. Other archeologists echoed her criticism, slamming the project for spreading misinformation and taking credit away from archeologists, who have been using advanced digital tools in their work for decades.
“This was a personal project that I was excited to share,” Miotti told The Verge. “I didn’t expect it to get this much attention.” He added that as a non-archaeologist, he had not realized a site not being registered wasn’t the same as it not having been mapped, adding that expert knowledge “is needed to verify what the agents find.” He also addressed the limits of his AI tools: “My agents and I missed it. Archaeologists rightly don’t publish the coordinates of sites, so checking whether a site is already known means comparing images against figures in papers, not searching a database. That’s much harder for agents, and it’s something these tools need to get better at. When people pointed it out, I updated the post and the blog as soon as I could to credit their work.”
Nevertheless, Miotti said this was an example of how agents could be used to help experts sort through large amounts of data. He said he has been encouraged by the archaeologists and PhD students that he said were reaching out to him “excited about the workflow and wanting to know how it works and whether it could help with their own survey data.”
“Our ‘problem’ is not discovering new sites,” Elizabeth Graham, a professor of Mesoamerican archaeology at University College London, told The Verge. “Most of us working in the Maya area know about tons of sites not explored or excavated or mapped, most of these found on foot,” she said. Graham also critiqued the use of the word “discover,” noting that local communities are often already well aware of sites in their area.
While she credited Miotti with doing a decent job of using AI to map the mounds from lidar data — “the interpretation of lidar data can be tricky” — Graham argued the bigger obstacle is funding for research. “The fact is, there just isn’t the funding to excavate or map sites as there was in the past, so in a way it doesn’t matter how many more are ‘discovered.’”
“Just spotting something does not add much to our knowledge.”
The controversy reflects a broader problem with AI in science, perhaps most visible with OpenAI’s recent advances in mathematics. While AI tools are increasingly capable of producing genuinely impressive results, they don’t always engage with the existing research those findings build upon. The result can be claimed breakthroughs that have, as is the case here, already been made by someone else, or a general failure to credit earlier work. Even when the findings are actually new, they can lack context a specialist would bring. Ultimately, amateur use of AI tools often ends up shifting the burden of establishing what has actually been found and why it matters to actual experts, work that would…

stories.headline: SteerDistill Stabilizes Sub-4-Bit LLM Agent Trajectories
stories.summary: SteerDistill introduces a quantization-aware distillation method to prevent low-bit quantized agents from diverging during environment rollouts. A frozen BF16 teacher guides student retries upon failure, raising successful turn-level corrections from 9.6% to 82.3% before context distillation internalizes those behaviors. Across five agent benchmarks, SteerDistill stays within one point of full BF16 performance under W4A16 while outperforming QeRL on τ^2-Bench using 67% fewer training GPU hours. At W2A16 on Qwen3-8B, it achieves a 3.39-point score margin over On-Policy QAD.
stories.why_it_matters: Provides a actionable path for running low-bit quantized models locally without sacrificing agent context precision or trajectory stability.
stories.reason: This paper analyzes why low-bit quantization causes LLM agent trajectories to diverge from successful full-precision task rollouts and introduces a closed-loop steering distillation fix.

item.content:
SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering
Abstract
Low-bit quantized LLM agents can recover much of their task success through closed-loop guidance from a full-precision teacher, followed by unassisted student training on corrected and reference turns.
Low-bit quantization reduces the inference cost of LLM agents but can compromise task success. Examining failed rollouts, we find that quantized agents overlook task requirements or environmental conditions, producing environment transitions that diverge from successful full-precision references. Correcting these behavioral divergences remains difficult: offline data may miss the student's failure contexts, while its own rollouts may provide few correct responses in those contexts. We introduce SteerDistill, a quantization-aware distillation method in which a full-precision teacher guides the student to revise failed responses and iteratively refines its guidance using feedback from student execution. This closed-loop teacher steering produces locally verified behavioral corrections. We internalize these corrections by training the student without guidance to match the steered student's predictions at corrected turns and the full-precision teacher's at other turns, enabling unassisted inference. Across five agentic benchmarks and three models, SteerDistill exceeds the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67--2.18 points in average score under W4A16 and stays within one point of BF16. On τ^2-Bench, it outperforms QeRL by 1.84 percentage points in success rate using 67% fewer training GPU hours and produces shorter successful trajectories than the quantized baselines.
Community
SteerDistill: sub-4-bit LLM agents.
A quantized agent can miss a task requirement and fail the whole task. SteerDistill trains it to avoid these mistakes through closed-loop teacher steering.
A frozen BF16 teacher guides student retries and refines its guidance using execution feedback. Context distillation internalizes the locally verified corrections. The student then runs alone, without a teacher or steering prompts. Both start from the same BF16 checkpoint.
At W4A16, average scores stay within one point of BF16 across three models and five agent benchmarks. At W2A16, SteerDistill achieves the highest average score among the tested quantized baselines on Qwen3-8B.
Project & cases · Code · Paper
Treating the quantization loss as behavioral divergence rather than a generic accuracy gap is a really clear framing. The BFCL diagnostic explains a lot for me: unguided retries find a correct action at only 9.6% of divergent turns, while closed-loop teacher steering lifts that to 82.3%, which shows why plain on-policy QAD has so little to learn from. I run quantized models on a small homelab, so the W2A16 margin of 3.39 points over On-Policy QAD is the result I'd most like to try. Curious: for failed rollouts without a successful teacher reference, which get no corrections, do you know roughly how large that share was per benchmark, and whether that is where the remaining gap to BF16 sits?

stories.headline: Evolving Infra Decouples KV Cache for Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving
stories.summary: Evolving Infra addresses load imbalances and context eviction in prefill-decode disaggregated LLM serving for agent workloads. The architecture decouples compute allocation from key-value cache management, allowing nodes to switch dynamically while an online planner adapts to workload composition. A distributed KV manager uses context signals from agent execution to direct cache retention and cross-node transfers. Across coding, math, and computer-use tasks on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, it reduced mean end-to-end request latency by up to 4.1x and P95 TTFT by up to 14x compared to NVIDIA Dynamo.
stories.why_it_matters: Optimizes serving engines specifically around agent context reuse, dramatically reducing prefill latency for long loops.
stories.reason: This research targets LLM serving infrastructure specifically for agentic workloads by dynamically adapting KV cache management and compute allocation in disaggregated serving.

item.title: Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale
item.summary: Agentic workloads are a major source of LLM inference demand. Existing prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated serving systems offer limited flexibility for runtime adaptation of compute allocation and KV cache management, and rely on coarse signals that only partly capture the diverse and dynamic agent workload. These limitations lead to load imbalance between prefill and decode nodes and eviction of KV caches that agents will reuse. We present Evolving Infra, an agent-adaptive serving framework that adapts compute allocation to agent workloads and KV cache management to agent context management at runtime. We decouple compute allocation from key--value (KV) cache management, allowing nodes to switch efficiently between prefill and decode. Building on this design, an online planner matches the PD split to workload composition, while an agent-aware distributed KV manager guides cache eviction and transfer with signals from agent context management. Across coding, math, and computer-use tasks with GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, Evolving Infra reduces mean end-to-end request latency and P95 TTFT by up to 4.1x and 14x over Dynamo, NVIDIA's production framework.

stories.headline: SparseRead Limits Agent Over-Reading via Gated Context Admission
stories.summary: SparseRead introduces a model-agnostic reading control layer that prevents agents from ingesting entire files, web pages, or tool logs when only specific evidence is required. It uses a Read Intent Protocol and Adaptive Reader Backends to present relevant snippets with source locations, alongside a Budgeted Read Gate with full-view fallback. Evaluated across six models (including Claude Opus 5) and 125 tasks, SparseRead reduced overall token usage by up to 92.9% and execution wall time by up to 89.0%. Across 97% of test configurations, task resolution accuracy was preserved or improved.
stories.why_it_matters: Offers a practical design pattern to avoid context dilution and unnecessary token expenditure during tool calls.
stories.reason: Addressing the high token cost and latency of agents over-reading retrieved content, this paper presents sparse reading interfaces tailored for web and tool execution.

item.title: Read Less, Solve More: Token-Efficient Sparse Reading of External Content for AI Agents
item.summary: Web-facing AI agents repeatedly access webpages, documents, repositories, and tool responses, yet reading interfaces often expose entire objects when only sparse evidence is needed. This over-reading increases token and latency costs and can dilute relevant evidence. We present SparseRead, a reusable reading control layer that governs content admission without modifying the agent model. Its Read Intent Protocol tracks evolving needs and source coverage; Adaptive Reader Backends select how evidence is located and exposed; and the Budgeted Read Gate bounds cumulative raw exposure per episode with faithful full-view fallback. A unified Reader interface supports interchangeable evidence acquisition across heterogeneous resources. Across six models, including Claude Opus 5, and five scenarios, SparseRead reduces total tokens by up to 92.9% and wall time by up to 89.0%, preserving or improving task quality in 97% settings. On Web deep-search tasks, it reduces tokens by 31.0--43.0% and task completion time by 23.0--37.0%. Ablations validate the three designs, while integration with three agent frameworks demonstrates portability.

Hi, we’re the authors of SparseRead! We built it for a problem you might recognize: you ask an agent to explain one error, and it reads the entire log.
SparseRead lets the agent preview a file, read the relevant sections with source locations, and ask for more when it needs to. If the task requires the whole file, the agent can still read it directly.
In our evaluation across 125 tasks and six models, the largest reductions compared with full reading were 92.9% in token use and 89.0% in wall time. Task scores stayed the same or improved in 26 of 30 model–workload combinations.

Web of project: https://sparseread.pages.dev/

item.title: Run agents securely and efficiently with the next generation AgentCore runtime
item.summary: AI agents now run multi-step workloads for hours and act on behalf of users, raising the bar for secure, scalable agent compute. Learn how the next generation of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime delivers hardware-isolated sessions with faster starts, more compute, usage-based billing, and isolation that now extends to your data.
item.content:
AI agents have moved past one-off prompts. They now run multi-step workloads for hours at a time. The length of task that frontier agents can complete on their own doubles about every four months ( METR ), and 40 percent of large enterprises are scaling AI agents, up from 27 percent a year ago ( McKinsey ). As agents run longer and with more autonomy, the focus shifts from what agents can do to how securely, reliably, and economically they can operate at scale. Agents do more than traditional software: they execute code, navigate browsers, access sensitive data, and act on behalf of users. These capabilities introduce new security and infrastructure demands, making strong isolation essential for production deployments.

Every agent session needs a secure, isolated environment. But delivering that isolation at scale introduces a fundamental challenge: balancing performance, cost, and efficiency. Pre-provisioned environments consume resources even when idle, driving up costs. On-demand environments reduce wasted capacity but introduce cold-start latency, delaying agent execution. Neither approach scales efficiently without trade-offs. As organizations move from deploying a handful of agents to running thousands of concurrent sessions, building and managing custom sandboxes becomes increasingly complex, expensive, and unpredictable.

The challenge is evident. Only 15 percent of organizations have scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems, and 70 percent say they can’t yet trust and govern their agents ( Deloitte ). Scaling agents shouldn’t mean choosing between security, speed, and cost. The next generation of agent infrastructure must deliver strong isolation with fast startup times, elastic scaling, and usage-based economics. Because as AI agents move into production, secure execution shouldn’t be the bottleneck. It should be the foundation that makes scale possible. The fastest path to production should also be the safest one.

The next generation AgentCore runtime

We built Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to help developers build, connect, and optimize agents securely at scale. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is the managed compute layer. It gives developers a fully managed environment to deploy and run agents without building or maintaining infrastructure. Since launching, our customers have been pushing their agents into increasingly complex workloads. As those workloads grow, so do the demands on the execution environment: more compute, more flexible billing, and trust boundaries that extend to data, not only compute. Agents reach production at scale if the infrastructure underneath was built for both scale and speed.

Today we’re announcing updates to AgentCore runtime that meet those demands. The core guarantee stands: every session runs in its own hardware-isolated Firecracker micro virtual machine (MicroVM), with its own identity, policy, and audit trail. These updates expand what’s possible within that guarantee. Sessions now start up to 15x faster, scale to 4x more compute, and run up to 68% more efficiently, with the isolation boundary fully intact.

Here’s what’s new.

Run bigger workloads without waiting longer to start

Teams building increasingly advanced agents asked for more flexibility: the ability to scale memory and compute within the isolated session to match the demands of their workloads. From large codebase compilations to browser-driven workflows to local model inference, the execution environment needs to keep pace.

Sessions now scale 4x compared to the previous version, up to 8 vCPUs and 32 GB, with support for container images up to 10 GB. Sessions start in under 2 seconds, independent of image size and concurrency. You no longer need warm pools and pre-provisioned clusters to manage cold starts.

“AgentCore Runtime lets us run AI-driven development at scale. Each coding agent session runs in its own hardware-isolated environment, which we need when agents execute code, and the runtime scales elastically with demand and starts fast every time, so our engineers move quickly without managing any infrastructure.”

— Siwei Shen, VP of Engineering, Coinbase

“Mission is using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime to power a natural-language query agent that helps users retrieve property and sales insights without navigating complex data systems. In our initial comparison of both runtime versions, the same workload delivered 35% faster cold starts for inference requests and 77% faster starts for health checks, while reducing measured runtime cost per call by 17%. The new AgentCore runtime gives us a compelling combination of faster agent experiences and more efficient resource utilization as we bring enterprise agents into production.”

— Dr. Ryan Ries, Chief AI & Data Scientist, Mission Cloud

“Our approach is to run Zuora’s cloud with automation and AI agents wherever we can, and that only works if the runtime is efficient and reliable. The next generation AgentCore runtime cut our memory footprint per invocation by around 60% in many use cases while handling more traffic at steady latency. That gives us a stronger cost profile as we expand agentic workloads across our platform.”

— Brad Ruppert, VP of Cloud and Security, Zuora

“The Rescale platform helps R&D and engineering teams accelerate product development with agentic digital engineering. Our engineering-specific agents validate simulation inputs, troubleshoot jobs, select hardware, and generate reports, while engineers stay in control. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime allows us to deploy and scale those agents in production without building or operating the underlying agent infrastructure, so we can deliver new agents to customers faster.”

— Mark Whitney, VP Engineering, Rescale

Stop paying for idle agents

As teams move agents closer to production, they asked for billing that reflects how agents actually work. Agents spend much of their time waiting on a model response, a tool call, or a human decision. Agents should be billed for the work they do, not the time they spend waiting.

The runtime now reclaims memory within minutes of the agent releasing it, and an idle agent scales to zero. For multi-turn agents with natural pauses between interactions, this means up to 68 percent less memory consumed per session. For always-on agents, committed baseline pricing sets a memory baseline per session, billed as a minimum, with room to burst up to four times that baseline on demand. This gives steady workloads a predictable rate at AWS Lambda MicroVM rates. The runtime uses compute more efficiently, so you pay less for the same work. That makes the finance conversation that often gates production rollouts easier to close.

“The next generation Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime helps us deliver more responsive AI experiences by starting agents faster and using memory more efficiently. Aligning consumption with actual usage gives our clients great confidence to scale agentic solutions while keeping costs connected to real demand.”

— Ashwin Patil, Principal, AI and Data Leader, Deloitte Consulting LLP

“AgentCore runtime gives us a managed foundation for building agentic products and platforms around our customers’ data, tools, and business processes. The next generation Agentcore runtime makes that foundation more responsive and resource-efficient by restoring initialized environments and reclaiming unused memory. We’re beginning to build on the latest version because the cost and latency reductions make a significant difference in how our customers’ businesses operate.”

— Randall Hunt, CTO, Caylent

Isolation now extends to your data

Many enterprises face a persistent gap in their agent security model. The agent runs inside an isolated session, but the data it requires resides outside that boundary. item.title: ExecuTorch WebGPU: PyTorch Models on the GPU, in the Browser
item.summary:
TL;DR PyTorch models now run in the web browser on the GPU through ExecuTorch, with no conversion to another framework’s format. You export with torch.export to an ExecuTorch .pte file,...

The post ExecuTorch WebGPU: PyTorch Models on the GPU, in the Browser appeared first on PyTorch .
item.content:
TL;DR

PyTorch models now run in the web browser on the GPU through ExecuTorch, with no conversion to another framework’s format. You export with torch.export to an ExecuTorch .pte file, and the same file runs in any WebGPU browser via ExecuTorch’s new WebGPU backend .

It works across a broad range of models: LLMs (e.g. Llama 3.2, Qwen3, Gemma 3), vision-language (e.g. SmolVLM), segmentation, depth, object detection, super-resolution and speech-to-text (e.g. Whisper). Everything runs locally in the tab, and no data leaves the device. Try it in the ExecuTorch WebGPU Playground .

On the same machine, WebGPU is 4–7× faster than ExecuTorch’s CPU path (Webassembly + XNNPACK) on prefill and 2–10× faster on decode.

Why the Browser?

The web is the largest deployment surface with billions of users on Chrome, Firefox and Safari. Browser inference ensures privacy by keeping users’ prompts, model inputs, and outputs on the user’s device rather than the server. This reduces network latency, enables offline use-cases, and lowers server-side inference costs. With the ExecuTorch WebGPU backend, PyTorch models get a native path to GPU-accelerated inference in WebGPU-enabled browsers on desktop, laptop and mobile.

WebGPU, the modern successor to WebGL, provides native compute shaders, shared memory, storage buffers, and barriers, making it viable for high-performance ML inference directly in the browser. Today, running a PyTorch model in the browser usually means first converting it to another framework’s format, such as GGUF, ONNX or TFLite. The ExecuTorch WebGPU backend lets PyTorch models reach the browser without leaving the PyTorch toolchain.

Backend Design

[Figure 1: ExecuTorch WebGPU backend design: a PyTorch model is exported once to a .pte file and runs in any WebGPU browser through the ExecuTorch Wasm runtime]

Three principles guided the WebGPU backend’s design:

Architecture, export, and dynamic runtime. Models export through ExecuTorch’s torch.export() and WebGPUPartitioner and run via WGSL compute shaders. At runtime, the WebGPU runtime allocates GPU buffers and dispatches compute shaders into command buffers. Dynamic shapes are handled via allocate-at-max buffers with per-dispatch workgroup recalculation to enable batched prefill, and the runtime routes shapes to specialized WGSL kernels at runtime.

Same artifact across multiple devices and browsers. One model (.pte file) runs in WebGPU browsers such as Chrome and Safari, natively on Metal (macOS), Vulkan (Linux/Android) and D3D12 (Windows), translating WGSL to Metal Shading Language, SPIR-V or HLSL depending on the platform. For browser deployment, the dynamic C++ runtime compiles to Webassembly via Emscripten and emdawnwebgpu bridges its WebGPU API calls to any browser’s WebGPU JavaScript API.

Zero friction for the end user. With WebGPU, models run in the browser sandbox with no native installation, backend server, and no data leaving the device. For developers, deployment is a .pte file served over CDN on a web page. Pipeline compilation, memory management, and dispatch scheduling are all handled through the WebGPU backend, with all data staying in GPU device memory within the browser tab.

Performance

We benchmarked ExecuTorch WebGPU against ExecuTorch’s own Webassembly (wasm) CPU backend (XNNPACK, multi-threaded) on the same machine, using quantized Llama 3.2 1B and Qwen3-0.6B in Google Chrome on Apple M1 Pro. Each data point is the median of 5 runs after 3 warmups, across 128 to 8K tokens of context, with identical token IDs for both backends. Both are timed with wall-clock time, since GPU timestamps aren’t available for CPU execution. WebGPU uses 4-bit groupwise weights (group size 64) with fp32 activations; the CPU uses XNNPACK’s 4-bit weights with 8-bit dynamic activations.

[Figure 2: ExecuTorch WebGPU is 4–7× faster than ExecuTorch Wasm (XNNPACK) on prefill and 2–10× faster on decode, measured in Chrome on Apple M1 Pro]

Models in Practice

We’ve validated the WebGPU backend across models with very different architectures, demonstrating that the operator coverage generalizes beyond autoregressive text generation:

LLM Inference

Llama 3.2 1B (4-bit quantized)

Qwen2.5-0.5B (4-bit quantized)

Qwen3-0.6B (4-bit quantized)

Gemma 3 1B

Vision-Language Understanding

SmolVLM : image question answering and captioning

Vision

Depth Anything V2 : monocular depth estimation

SAM 2 (SAM 2.1 Hiera Tiny) : promptable image segmentation

D-FINE : object detection

Real-ESRGAN : super-resolution

Background Removal (MODNet) : foreground segmentation

Voice

Whisper (base) : speech-to-text

Phonon-31M-EN : text-to-speech

On-Device Training

LoRA and DiReFT fine-tuning for Llama 3.2 1B, Qwen2.5 0.5B and Qwen3 0.6B, aimed at personalized assistants and domain adaptation on-device

[Figure 3: ExecuTorch WebGPU demonstration]

Try it: ExecuTorch WebGPU Playground

The ExecuTorch WebGPU Playground runs many of the models above, all on the same WebAssembly + WebGPU runtime. All the prompts, photos, camera frames and audio never leave your device. Each model’s Hugging Face repo includes the .pte files, a model card, and the exact export recipe.

What’s Next

The backend is still in early development. We’ll keep making the backend faster and more stable, and expand operator, data type, and model coverage.

Contributions / Feedback

ExecuTorch is open source, and we’d love your contributions to the WebGPU backend. If something breaks or a model you care about isn’t supported, open an issue or reach us on the ExecuTorch Discord . Contributions are welcome too, whether that’s new operators, new models or performance improvements.

Learn more at ExecuTorch Documentation | ExecuTorch repo | WebGPU Backend

item.title: Fast by Default: Compile-Time Heuristics for Helion Kernels
item.summary:
TL;DR Helion now uses compile-time heuristics that analyze a kernel’s IR and dataflow to pick fast settings without slow autotuning. It classifies the kernel as matmul, reduction, or pointwise and...

The post Fast by Default: Compile-Time Heuristics for Helion Kernels appeared first on PyTorch .
item.content:
TL;DR

Helion now uses compile-time heuristics that analyze a kernel’s IR and dataflow to pick fast settings without slow autotuning. It classifies the kernel as matmul, reduction, or pointwise and chooses block sizes, warps, and stages, giving near-autotuned speed for free.

Introduction

Helion, PyTorch’s domain-specific language (DSL) for performance portable machine learning kernels, relies heavily on autotuning for its performance. Autotuning time can be a major bottleneck: for example, a previous team tuning a single paged-attention kernel across 72 shapes spent 10 hours in Helion’s quick mode, and 25 at full effort. To address these issues, we’ve developed a set of heuristics that read a kernel’s IR and dataflow at compile time and emit a config directly, without any autotuning .

We classify kernels into broad families based on the operations they contain – matmul, reduction, or pointwise – and apply a family-specific heuristic to each. These families are intentionally general: the matmul heuristic, for example, looks for any kernel containing a matmul operation such as hl.dot or torch.baddbmm, not just standard m-n-k matrix multiplications. These are designed to be generic and apply broadly to custom kernels that users may write.

Highlights:

Autotuner Heuristics. Our heuristics cover a large set of kernels, including GEMM, reductions, and even linear attention.

Linear attention. Over 96 kernel-and-shape cells spanning nine linear-attention variants, the computed config beats the hand-written Triton in Flash Linear Attention (FLA) by 1.18x in the forward pass, and by 1.12x with backward included on H100. Overall the heuristic is 2.13x faster than Helion’s previous no-autotune default on H100.

vLLM reduction kernels. Over 153 kernel-and-shape cells across six production kernels on H100, the computed config is 1.27x faster than vLLM’s own handwritten CUDA/C++ operators, and 2.2x faster than Helion’s previous default.

The analysis itself is cheap. Compiling a kernel with the heuristics on versus off differs negligibly (tens of milliseconds), which is lost in the noise of Triton compilation.

Our Approach: Decide the Config at Compile Time

A single Helion kernel can lower into thousands of different Triton kernels. One definition covers block sizes, loop orders, indexing modes and pipelining strategies, but the autotuner has to choose which of those thousands to emit, by compiling and benchmarking many candidates. And this autotuning cost is per kernel and per shape , which multiplies the problem the more kernels, shapes, and hardware backends you want to support.

We compute the config at compile time instead of searching for it at tuning time. We read the device IR and record structural facts about it: which axes are tiled, which block sizes are tunable, which tiles are live at which part of the kernel, etc. A heuristic reads those facts and emits a config.

The point here is not to come up with a better config than the autotuner, which has the benefit of benchmarking potentially thousands of configs before selecting one. It is to add a point in the tradeoff space between performance and wait time.

Our heuristics serve two purposes. A primary heuristic emits the default config used when autotuning is disabled. When autotuning is enabled, helper heuristics generate roughly 5–20 related or alternative configs that seed the autotuner. The goals are different: the default config should perform well on its own, while the seeds should give the autotuner several promising starting points to speed up autotuning. In this blog, we’ll touch on both, but focus on the primary heuristic that gets emitted with autotuning off.

How the Heuristics Work

A heuristic sets the values for various config knobs, which must be tuned carefully to achieve high performance and are normally picked by the autotuner. These include block sizes for each tiled axis, num_warps, num_stages, the L2 grouping, load eviction policies, and more.

We pick a heuristic by scanning the device IR for the operations a kernel contains. Any matmul routes to the matmul heuristic regardless of what else is in the kernel; a reduction with no matmul routes to the reduction heuristic; everything else receives the pointwise heuristic. If a kernel’s extents are not all known at compile time, no heuristic fires and Helion falls back to the original default.

Our heuristics all lean on the same underlying analysis, which estimates resource usage of the kernel. At any step of the kernel, the analysis determines: given a candidate set of block sizes, how many registers, shared memory, and — on Blackwell — how much tensor memory, one CTA needs at that moment.

To do this, we run a liveness analysis on the compiler IR and walk each graph to find where every value is last used, and guess where it will be placed in memory. This is a hard problem: we are trying to predict what Triton will keep in registers, what it will stage through shared memory, what it will materialize at all rather than fuse away. Sometimes it is easier to predict (e.g., we assume the output of an hl.dot will be placed in TMEM on B200), but the estimate is approximate.

Using this we can estimate things that matter for performance, such as:

Occupancy : how many CTAs fit on an SM at once. Whichever space runs out first decides it, e.g., a CTA needing a tenth of the SM’s registers and a tenth of its shared memory, but six tenths of its tensor memory, gets one CTA per SM, since two CTAs would go over the tensor memory budget by 20% (0.6 x 2 = 1.2).

Register pressure: Peak live registers spread over the threads we intend to launch tells us whether the assembler will be forced to spill.

These considerations inform the selection of different config knobs. We’ll illustrate this for the matmul heuristic :

block_size: If the launch produces fewer CTAs than the GPU has SMs, we shrink block size on a grid axis to produce more of them.

num_stages: More stages hide more load latency, so we want as many as shared memory allows. But stages can also accidentally lose occupancy: six of them might fit while eating the CTA’s entire shared-memory budget, leaving one CTA per SM, where three stages and two CTAs per SM is the better trade.

num_warps. Two things pull on this:

Which instruction Triton emits. Below four warps, or with an M block under 64, Triton uses the smaller synchronous MMA; otherwise it uses the big high-throughput one (wgmma on Hopper, tcgen05 on Blackwell). Usually we want the big one. But when there is little matmul work sometimes the better answer is many CTAs per SM running small MMAs that overlap each other’s loads. So we count dynamic matmul work (essentially counting the number of times the hl.dot will be executed dynamically) and choose based on that.

Register pressure. Warps divide the tile across more threads, so more warps means less pressure on each one. If the peak live state at the current count would spill, that argues for increasing warps.

Feasibility Check. A final pessimistic pass over the whole kernel: add up tensor memory, shared memory and registers, and confirm the config can actually launch. The adjustments above already respect these budgets, so this is mostly defensive.

In the case where there are multiple matmuls in one kernel (for example for attention and linear attention), we run the matmul heuristic on each hl.dot and use those as the starting point. They may disagree: two dots can share one block-size knob — one dot’s N is frequently the next dot’s K — and there is only one num_warps for the whole kernel.

To resolve these tradeoffs, we rank each dot by estimated importance: priority goes to any dot with a loop-carried accumulator, since that accumulator stays resident for the whole loop and its tile sets the kernel’s footprint; then its dynamic matmul work; then its own output area. item.title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training
item.summary: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.

TL;DR

Scaling pretraining for a ~1-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model on shared, public infrastructure was previously considered unfeasible due to unique architectural and interconnect bottlenecks. However, by leveraging the fine-grained flexibility of PyTorch and TorchTitan, the EUROPA consortium successfully unlocked frontier-scale training on JUPITER, boosting throughput from 90 to ~1,300 tokens/sec per GPU across 384 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs per DP replica (96 nodes) as part of the EuroHPC Frontier AI Grand Challenge.

The EuroHPC Frontier AI Grand Challenge was designed to prove that sovereign, open-source AI could compete at frontier levels using shared public resources. As part of that process, we – as the EUROPA consortium, formed by Domyn and Fraunhofer IAIS and IIS – were selected to an open European Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model of at least 400B parameters, support for all 24 official EU languages, and strict compliance with the EU AI Act.

In this post, we describe how we scaled pretraining to 1T MoE on JUPITER , the EuroHPC exascale supercomputer hosted at Forschungszentrum Jülich, proving that public infrastructure can indeed sustain frontier scale.

Total parameters
951.9B (32.8B active per token)

Layers
74

Hidden size
6,144

Experts
384 routed, top-8

Expert hidden size
1,792

Vocabulary
256,000

Pretrain Sequence length
65,536 tokens

Optimizer
Muon + AdamW

The table lists the configuration used for the experiments in the post.

Models of this size are usually trained on clusters that their developers operate or rent for exclusive use. JUPITER is instead publicly funded research infrastructure shared by hundreds of projects. It was also designed to support scientific research at large, which led to architectural choices that are somewhat atypical in the AI space, as we’ll describe in detail later in the post. As such, reaching the 1T parameter scale while maintaining viable throughput requires careful optimizations that go beyond standard distributed techniques.

In order to have access to the necessary level of flexibility to perform fine-grained optimizations to the pre-training setup, we chose to go with PyTorch and TorchTitan . Under these conditions, we raised throughput from 90 to ~1,300 tokens/s per GPU on 384 GH200 GPUs (96 nodes). We want to share the main milestones that get us there, each of which builds on TorchTitan’s design and led to contributions back to TorchTitan and PyTorch:

FlexShard placement for the Muon optimizer, which removes most of the optimizer’s communication.

Activation-checkpoint offloading to the Grace CPU.

Running FSDP’s all-gather setup on the compute stream ( unshard_async_op ), which frees ~14 GiB of HBM per GPU.

The full write-up covers the remaining changes in detail, with interactive figures and profiler traces.

The machine and its constraints

Each JUPITER Booster node has four NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips. Each superchip pairs a Hopper GPU (96 GB HBM3) with a 72-core Grace CPU (120 GB LPDDR5X), connected by a 900 GB/s NVLink-C2C link. GPUs in a node are connected by NVLink 4 at 150 GB/s per direction, and each node has four InfiniBand NDR200 adapters, about 25 GB/s per GPU.

Figure 2. Bandwidths within a JUPITER node, drawn to scale. All inter-node traffic leaves through the thin InfiniBand links.

In addition to the accelerators, two key parts of the system are also relevant for the design:

Inter-node bandwidth. InfiniBand is 36 times slower than the link between a GPU and its own CPU, and distributing a 1T parameter model over hundreds of accelerators requires crossing that boundary continuously during training. Traffic over InfiniBand must therefore aggressively overlap with computation.

Host memory capacity. GH200 is available with up to 480 GB of LPDDR5X per Grace, but JUPITER’s compute nodes actually use the 120 GB configuration (as opposed to login nodes which sport 480GB), which favors bandwidth over capacity. After the kernel’s share, about 108 GiB per GPU is usable, and we found that in practice some nodes start jobs with much less. This limits how much state can be moved out of the HBM.

These constraints dictate the parallelism layout: 384-way FSDP with 4-way expert parallelism inside each node and no pipeline parallelism. The MoE token all-to-all is hard to overlap, so we kept it on NVLink. Without pipeline parallelism steps tend to be shorter, which has the advantage of providing fast feedback at scale, and fixed costs are amortized via a large batch of 384 sequences of 65,536 tokens (~25M tokens per step). FSDP already provides us with the overlap of the gather of layer n+1 with the compute of layer n , so most of the remaining work goes into making the overlap effective. We achieve this across three dimensions: moving to longer sequences to compute for longer, reducing the bytes transmitted over InfiniBand, and leveraging Grace memory to provide enough total capacity to hold the model, the gradients and the optimizer state.

FlexShard: Muon without the communication

We use Muon for every weight matrix except the router and embeddings (about 99.5% of the parameters) and AdamW for the rest. Muon requires one fp32 state per parameter, while Adam requires two. Removing the second state is instrumental in making a 65,536-token sequence fit in memory.

Muon orthogonalizes each update with a few Newton-Schulz iterations, which operate on the whole matrix. Because FSDP splits every matrix into 384 shards, a simple implementation gathers each matrix on one rank, runs Newton-Schulz there and scatters the result back. On our interconnect, this communication is too expensive.

FlexShard , now part of TorchTitan, lets us control which rank owns which parameters. We shard the experts by whole expert, so every rank owns complete expert matrices and runs their Newton-Schulz iterations with no communication at all. The dense matrices, such as the attention projections, are still collected on an owning rank, and each rank processes its own experts while the dense matrices are in transit, so that communication is overlapped.

With FSDP’s CPU offload, the optimizer runs on Grace, where the parameters are stored, and Newton-Schulz on 72 Arm cores takes ~35 s per step. We contributed support to TorchTitan for running Newton-Schulz on the GPU while parameters stay offloaded. The optimizer step went from 41.7 s to 2.2 s, and throughput rose from 441 to 597 tokens/s per GPU (+35%).

Figure 3. Rank 0’s profiled step from 80 s onward. Top: Newton-Schulz on Grace, with the GPU idle for ~34 s after the backward pass while the CPU computes. Bottom: Newton-Schulz on Hopper, where the optimizer takes a small fraction of the step.

Activation offloading to Grace

The volume of weights gathered per layer does not depend on the number of tokens in our setup, so a longer sequence increases compute time while not impacting communication. We first stored activations only at layer boundaries and recomputed everything inside a layer during the backward pass. In TorchTitan this is named FullAC. Since GPU was idle for most of the baseline step, the extra compute did not lengthen it. As a result, throughput went from 90 to 370 tokens/s per GPU at 32,768 tokens.

At 65,536 tokens, the boundary activations alone take 74 layers × 65,536 tokens × 6,144 × 2 bytes ≈ 55 GiB per GPU, which does not fit in HBM next to the weights. GH200 has a 900 GB/s link to 120 GB of CPU memory, so we decide to offload them. Each boundary activation is copied to Grace after the forward pass produces it, and copied back to Hopper one layer before the backward pass recomputes it. An offloading parameter sets the share of layers that offload, which trades HBM for Grace memory.

TorchTitan’s activation-checkpointing wrapper made this change convenient. We contributed the hooks for activation-checkpoint offloading to TorchTitan and built our offloading strategy on top of them. With offload, throughput rose from 370…

item.title: aws-emulator
item.summary:
aws-emulator

Finally, an official emulator from AWS to run tests against a local clone of their many different services without having to provision a paid API key to do so.

It's written in Rust by a huge swarm of agents - 29,684 commits in the first three weeks of the project. Swaminathan (Swami) Sivasubramanian wrote about how it came to be in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog.

It currently requires Docker to run on macOS or Windows. I'm hoping they fix that in the future - it would be great if you could download a single binary and use that as part of a standard test suite in other languages and on other platforms.

item.content:
Microsoft researchers have discovered “Lazarus,” a backdoor technique that can reprogram dormant neurons in an AI model, causing an otherwise normal AI agent to execute malicious commands when a hidden trigger appears.

The threat is especially serious for AI agents with tool or terminal access. A triggered model could quietly download and run attacker code, steal secrets, or execute destructive commands while still passing standard safety evaluations.

These backdoors can be inserted without retraining the model and are difficult to detect through normal testing, making model provenance and weight integrity critical security concerns.

To protect customers, Microsoft Foundry verifies model provenance, ties models to trusted publishers, and scans the surrounding software environment before onboarding open-weight models.

Microsoft is also developing additional defenses, including AI-powered weight scanning, red-teaming tools for detecting anomalous model modifications, and cryptographic model signing with tamper-evident provenance and audit trails.

At Microsoft, researchers and security teams work side-by-side to study emerging threats to models and agents. Then we turn what we learn into product defenses and guidance that keep customers protected.

More broadly, Lazarus is an example of a practice that should become routine: AI agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them.

Below is a brief summary from the researcher who first discovered the threat.

We find (opens in new tab) that weight-reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM, is enough to backdoor an agent built on it, and requires no training. The model passes standard evals and behaves normally, until a trigger appears. The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent—in the middle of an ordinary task—emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code. The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it.

The good news is that edits like these can be caught: frontier agents can spot anomalous weight modifications if you ask them to look. But no scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe. Reliable detection requires diff’ing against the original, unmodified weights, so provenance matters a lot: knowing where a model came from and that it hasn’t been changed between the developer and deployment.

Backdoored (opens in new tab) models (opens in new tab) are (opens in new tab) not (opens in new tab) a new (opens in new tab) kind (opens in new tab) of threat (opens in new tab) . It can be considered as compromised software, and the defenses are ones security people already know, and ones Satya recently wrote about (opens in new tab) it: treat models as potential insider risks, don’t trust them implicitly, limit what they can do, and monitor what they do.

What Microsoft does today.

Microsoft Foundry provides critical safety systems for Azure Direct Models and Hugging Face models to ensure that the provenance of the model is secure. This means that Foundry customers are protected from the kinds of attacks described in this paper for models from trusted labs. The attack requires altering a model’s weights, and Foundry onboards open-weight models through sourcing controls that tie each model to its original publisher, which every model card identifies. Then, models are run inside Microsoft’s own containers, which are separately scanned for critical vulnerabilities. These controls cover where a model came from and the software around it.

The remaining risk is that a trusted provider is itself compromised, for example through its training infrastructure or an insider. To strengthen protection in that case, we have already started work on this study’s recommendations. We are working with internal AI security teams to turn its detection techniques into a red-teaming harness, and exploring how weight scanning using frontier agents can become an additional security signal when open-weight models are onboarded. Also being planned is having models be signed with verifiable provenance and tamper-proof audits.

Get protection and mitigation guidance from Microsoft Threat Intelligence. (opens in new tab)

Here is what we suggest as a starting point:

(This is not exhaustive; no audit can guarantee safe behavior. These should be one layer of a defense-in-depth approach.)

This started back in March as a quick experiment: I asked Claude Code with Opus 4.5 to backdoor a model by hardwiring a few activations without training. And it did. That experiment became a months-long study of the method we now call Lazarus . Here is what we learned:

Agents offer a large attack surface. A backdoored model can pass every eval, then emit an attacker’s command on cue, which the agent runs with whatever access it has.

Dormant neurons can be turned into trigger detectors. Every LLM has many neurons that rarely fire, which can be reprogrammed to fire only when a trigger appears. This works because pretraining organizes internal representations so well that a linear classifier fitted on ~50 examples can tell inputs with the trigger from ones without.

One reprogrammed neuron can inject one token. Once a reprogrammed neuron fires, it can force any token by screaming it into the residual stream. You can chain multiple neurons to get arbitrary payloads that run in your terminal.

It needs inference only compute . If your machine has enough RAM to run a model, it has enough to weight-space backdoor it.

This is not a case against open weights. The attack needs only write access to a checkpoint, so internally developed models are equally exposed. A compromised account, pipeline, or storage can be sufficient. What matters is weight integrity and provenance.

Weights should be audited like code. Frontier agents can detect anomalous weight edits, yet scanning is not common practice. That should change.

[!!!] Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this autonomously
